NoteTexAccessor::sub_norm¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note NoteTexAccessor::sub_norm() const

Brace Every Bare Subscript¶

sub_norm() wraps every unbraced subscript — _x, a run of one or more ASCII letters/digits, or _\alpha, a single control word — in explicit braces: _{x}, _{\alpha}. Use it before further TeX processing that only recognizes the braced form, or to normalize source that mixes _x and _{x} for the same conceptual subscript.

The match is greedy over the whole following alnum run, not just one character. x_1b becomes x_{1b}, not x_{1}b — there is no boundary between a digit and a following letter, so 1b is captured as one subscript. Write x_1 b (a space) if the digit and the letter are meant to be a script and separate following text.

A subscript already wrapped in braces — _{already} — is left untouched; there is no second pass to normalize its interior. A control word subscript (_\alpha) captures the whole word, matching how \alpha is one token even though it is not itself alphanumeric before the backslash.

The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note. Undefined input remains undefined; Bool, Int64, Float64, and Bytes receivers are rejected because TeX source is Text.

Example 1: Bare, Control-Word, And Already-Braced Forms¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"x_1 + y_ab + z_\\alpha + w_{already}"})
              .tex().sub_norm()
          << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["x_{1} + y_{ab} + z_{\\alpha} + w_{already}"]

Example 2: The Greedy Run Captures Digit And Letter Together¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"a_1b_2", "no subs here"})
              .tex().sub_norm()
          << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["a_{1b}_{2}", "no subs here"]

a_1b_2 has two subscript starts (_1b and _2), each captured as far as the run of alnum characters extends — 1b together, then 2 alone.

Example 3: Undefined And Non-Text Input¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << pluss::Note::undefined().tex().sub_norm().defined()
          << '\n';
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2}).tex().sub_norm();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

false
Int64: rejected

See Also¶

  • sup_norm: the identical bracing rule applied to ^ instead of _.

  • prime_norm: rewrites trailing ' marks into an explicit ^{...} superscript, a related but distinct normalization.
